fetched_contents.text: Developing a 3D strategy: Pipelines and recommendations for 3D structured light scanning of archaeological artefacts Under a Creative Commons license Open access Abstract Archaeology has faced increased pressure to digitise collections and make artefacts available and accessible to a wider audience. 3D imaging involves producing a 3D digital or printed model of an object or site. 3D models have the potential to augment the traditional approaches to museum engagement whilst breaking down the barriers to access, whether through providing 3D printed proxies in museums or sharing digital models online. 3D imaging has clear value in archaeology and public engagement but there is no standardisation or accessible pipelines available for achieving professional 3D imaging output. There is very little consensus in 3D modelling and worldwide, digital collections are being created with no methodological consistency. This research observed each stage necessary for producing high-quality 3D models with structured light scanning (SLS) technology. SLS was effective on a range of textures that may be encountered in archaeological scenarios, although highly reflective objects, or pale objects with black areas, may fail to be captured even with an altered strategy. In order to make the 3D model most representative of the archaeological find, it is recommended that a range of scanner settings such as brightness or shutter speed are tested on the object before committing these settings to the rest of the scans. Generalised 3D scanning pipelines are provided to inform archaeological teams on a 3D digital and printing strategy. * Previous * Next Keywords 3D imaging 3D printing Method Structured light scanning Museum 1. Introduction 3D imaging has seen rapid development and increased awareness through recent years, emerging as an invaluable technique for archaeological projects and digital archaeology by encouraging a new dimension toward recording and analysing finds (Tanasi, 2020; Wessels et al., 2022). 3D imaging technologies have seen significant development in quality, speed, affordability and user friendliness that have reduced the barriers of entry caused by complicated or highly technical methodologies and expensive equipment (Athanasiou et al., 2013; Campana and Remondino, 2008; Hirst et al., 2018; Kaiser and Dědič, 2024; Pavelka et al., 2021; Rusinkiewicz et al., 2002; Siebke et al., 2018). However, there is still very little methodological consistency observed in 3D scanning strategies for producing digital collections. Modern 3D scanners have the capacity to meet the capture and reproduction needs for archaeological casework; they are accurate, rapid, portable, relatively low cost, and have user-friendly assembly and interface (Bruno et al., 2010; Kaiser and Dědič, 2024; Remondino and Rizzi, 2010). A detailed discussion of 3D scanning technologies is provided by Carew and Errickson (2019). However, guidance and recommendations for 3D scanning procedures are currently limited, resulting in the absence of standardisation across 3D specialists, professionals and beginners (Raneri, 2018). For example, Kuzminsky and Gardiner (2012) provided a detailed discussion on the potential and process for digital measurements of laser-scanned bones, but limited information on setup considerations, scan processing, or digital hosting procedures. Historic England (Historic England, 2018, 2024) highlighted the stages of scanning and post-processing with some considerations provided, with exceptional value to terrestrial landscape and building capture. Alternatively, Cerasoni et al. (2022) compiled resources for producing photogrammetry-derived models, which results in good quality textures but omits the precise topographic measurements integrated with 3D imaging technologies. However, there is still an urgent need for accessible scanning guidelines from initial object through to the final deliverable; furthermore, there is limited consensus in 3D modelling protocols for creating digital collections of different artefacts. This paper explores the 3D SLS capture of different textures to inform the suitability of 3D scanning on different objects, with generalised but comprehensive pipelines for producing 3D digital and printed models for professional heritage output and to inspire further articles into 3D imaging pipelines with alternative technologies. 1.1. Technologies for 3D scanning object surfaces 3D imaging can involve the capture of the internal structure of an object via medical techniques such as 3D ultrasound and computerised tomography (CT) or capture of the object surface via laser and light scanners. Briefly, laser scanners, whether based on time-of-flight, phase shift or triangulation technology, use laser lines to measure the distance between the scanner and individual points of the object to produce a 3D cloud of data points (Howland, 2018; Sansoni et al., 2009). Structured light scanners (SLS) project calibrated white and blue light patterns that measure and photograph the entire targeted area (Jecić and Drvar, 2003; Opitz, 2013). Both technologies construct a single digital model by collecting and aligning or registering these individual scans of the object surface together (Lerma et al., 2010; Opitz, 2013; Williams et al., 2019). Some 3D scanners also offer hybrid light and laser modes which take advantage of the laser accuracy and surface suitability alongside light texture capture. Whilst the terms ‘3D mesh’ and ‘3D model’ are used interchangeably, a mesh is specifically the connected geometry of the scans, made up of individual vertices and faces, whereas a 3D model is a collection of one or more meshes with post-processed lighting and textures. This research focuses on SLS rather than laser modalities because SLS scanners are cheaper, more accessible, and routinely capture high-quality textures, bringing significant benefit to archaeological practice. Submission received: 7 May 2025 / Revised: 26 June 2025 / Accepted: 1 July 2025 / Published: 9 July 2025 Abstract The last decade has seen a transformative advancement in computational technologies, enabling the precise creation, evaluation, visualization, and reproduction of high-fidelity three-dimensional (3D) models of archaeological sites and artefacts. With the advent of 3D printing, both small- and large-scale objects can now be reproduced with remarkable accuracy and at customizable scales. Artefacts composed of organic materials—such as wood—are inherently susceptible to biological degradation and thus require extensive, long-term conservation employing costly methodologies. These procedures often raise environmental concerns and lead to irreversible alterations in the wood’s chemical composition, dimensional properties, and the intangible essence of the original artefact. In the context of public education and the dissemination of knowledge about historical technologies and objects, 3D replicas can effectively fulfill the same purpose as original artefacts, without compromising interpretative value or cultural significance. Furthermore, the digital data embedded in 3D surface and object models provides a wealth of supplementary information that cannot be captured, preserved, or documented through conventional techniques. Waterlogged wooden objects can now be thoroughly documented in 3D, enabling ongoing, non-invasive scientific analysis. Given these capabilities, it is imperative to revisit the philosophical and ethical foundations of preserving waterlogged wood and to adopt innovative strategies for the conservation and presentation of wooden artefacts. These new paradigms can serve educational, research, and outreach purposes—core functions of contemporary museums. 1. Introduction Wood has held deep significance throughout human history. The earliest references to its care appear in the 4000-year-old Epic of Gilgamesh [1], rooted in Babylonian–Sumerian tradition, where tar oil is mentioned as a protective agent for wood. Similarly, Sanskrit hymns from the Rigveda advise on the best season for tree felling to ensure longevity [2]. Early records of archaeology and conservation appear on a cuneiform tablet from Larsa (Iraq), detailing how Kings Nebuchadnezzar II and Nabonidus searched for traces of earlier rulers. Nabonidus reportedly discovered inscriptions from King Hammurabi during a temple excavation. The Larsa tablet and a terracotta cylinder describe restoration work on the Temple of Shamash in Larsa between 555 and 539 BCE [3]. Remarkably, Princess Ennigaldi-Nanna, daughter of Nabonidus, collected and preserved artefacts—wooden ones included—making the Temple of Shamash the world’s first museum [4]. In 2002 during archaeological investigations in the riverbed of the Ljubljanica near Sinja Gorica, a remarkable discovery was made among various remains—a small, hand-crafted wooden point resembling Paleolithic stone tools. The point, made from yew wood (Taxus baccata), was subjected to dual radiocarbon dating (Oxford, Beta), which determined its age to be approximately 40,000 years. Owing to an unusual and fortunate series of events, the object was preserved in sediment with minimal physical, biological, or chemical interference that might have otherwise led to its deterioration [5,6]. 2. Materials and Methods This study employed comparative analysis of conservation methods using case studies, including the Paleolithic wooden point and a Roman barge. Three-dimensional scanning techniques such as CT and photogrammetry were used for documentation. Conservation outcomes were assessed through volumetric analysis and visual inspection. However, reburial as a conservation strategy must be assessed on a case-by-case basis, since some agents of deterioration—especially certain bacteria and fungi—may persist or even thrive under specific anaerobic conditions [7]. Therefore, environmental characterization and risk assessment are essential before implementing reburial. Therefore, our proposal should be regarded as a viable alternative and considered alongside existing conservation methods. It was decided, unfortunately in our opinion, to conserve the Paleolithic wooden point using a conventional method—melamine resin treatment—based on standards established 40 to 60 years ago. Despite the passage of time, professional conservation practices have changed little. In contrast, digital documentation has progressed rapidly, now allowing for complete digital reconstruction and replication [8,9,10,11,12]. Section 5 provides a detailed analysis of how the melamine-based preservation process was carried out. Several 3D models of the wooden point were captured using a CT scanner before, during, and after the melamine conservation process, and were subsequently compared. It is our professional and scientific responsibility to preserve cultural heritage for future generations. Photogrammetry has become a valuable tool for waterlogged wood, but its effectiveness is constrained by the material’s physical and environmental properties. The evidence indicates that photogrammetry can reliably capture the overall geometry and texture of waterlogged archaeological wood, including fine surface details and color information, provided the imaging system is calibrated appropriately [N1-F1]. The same source also emphasizes that photogrammetry can provide “high resolution and accuracy” if calibrated, and that it is useful for monitoring waterlogged wood in conservation liquids [N1-F1]. This is important because waterlogged wood is often difficult to image due to its moisture content and lack of rich texture, which complicates Structure-from-Motion (SfM) techniques [N1-F1].

A major limitation imposed by moisture is that waterlogged wood may not provide enough identifiable surface features for reliable photogrammetric reconstruction [N1-F1]. The same source notes that the surface may not provide rich texture, making SfM techniques difficult to apply [N1-F1]. In addition, water and conservation liquids introduce optical interferences such as reflections, chromatic aberration, refraction at air–water interfaces, and turbidity, all of which degrade image quality [N1-F1]. These issues are particularly severe in a multimedia environment where refraction and scale definition are critical [N1-F1]. The evidence also highlights that ambient lighting can be excluded or controlled in specialized setups, such as nighttime measurements, to reduce interference [N1-F1].

Lighting and texture are especially important because photogrammetry depends on visible surface features to generate dense point clouds and textured models. The source explicitly states that the wood surface must be handled carefully, respecting conservation ethics, and that commercial adhesives on the surface are not possible because of the wood’s sensitivity to drying and conservation treatments [N1-F1]. This means that photogrammetry can be degraded by poor lighting, poor texture, and the need to avoid damaging the object during imaging. The evidence also suggests that specialized lighting and camera setups are needed to mitigate turbidity and refraction [N1-F1].

Software and hardware choices play a decisive role in improving or degrading results. The source reports that refraction correction is imperative for good results, and that scale definition with highly accurately determined scale bars and relative orientation constraints improve accuracy [N1-F1]. It also notes that indirect flat lighting was used to mitigate turbidity [N1-F1]. These technical choices show that photogrammetry can be made more reliable through careful hardware design, calibration, and software processing. The evidence also implies that general 3D scanning pipelines and scanner settings should be tested on the object before committing them to the rest of the scans [N2-F2], though this advice is more general to 3D scanning than specifically to photogrammetry.

Overall, photogrammetry is useful for capturing shape, color, and texture on waterlogged wood, but it is limited by the wood’s moisture, lack of rich texture, and optical interferences from water and conservation environments [N1-F1]. Its performance depends heavily on controlled lighting, refraction correction, scale bars, and relative orientation constraints, and it is especially vulnerable to poor surface texture and turbid imaging conditions [N1-F1]. For waterlogged wood, photogrammetry is therefore a powerful but highly sensitive method that can improve visualization only when the imaging setup is optimized for the material’s constraints [N1-F1].

Laser scanning offers a different set of strengths and limitations for waterlogged wood. The evidence shows that laser scanning can reliably capture the precise 3D geometry of waterlogged archaeological wood, including surface detail and repeatable measurements over time [N2-R3]. One source explicitly states that terrestrial laser scanning enables accurate three-dimensional recording of fragile wet-preserved archaeological wood, and repeat scanning reveals immersion-related changes [N2-R3]. Another source notes that laser scanning records the distance from the scanner to points on a surface using eye-safe lasers, generating a point cloud [N2-R4]. This makes laser scanning especially suitable for capturing stable, repeatable measurements and for documenting fragile wood that may not tolerate physical contact.

A major limitation imposed by water is that waterlogged wood is often submerged or surrounded by conservation liquids, which can affect the scanning environment and introduce challenges such as reflections, refraction, and turbidity [N1-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that waterlogged wood is prone to deformation and decay if not stabilized immediately after recovery [N1-F1], which means scanning must often be done in controlled conservation settings rather than in open-air conditions. Additionally, the source notes that the conservation liquid surrounding the wood can over the course of treatment cause deformation, rotation, local degradation, and other optical interferences on images observing the wood [N1-F1]. This indicates that the physical condition of the wood and the surrounding liquid can both degrade scan quality.

Surface condition and scan environment are also important constraints. The evidence notes that laser scanners use laser lines to measure distance to points on the object and that modern scanners are accurate, rapid, and relatively low cost [N2-F2]. However, it also cautions that highly reflective objects or pale objects with black areas may fail to be captured even with altered strategies [N2-F2]. For waterlogged wood, the surface may be damp, wet, or covered by conservation fluids, which can affect reflectivity and scanning consistency. The source also states that laser scanners can be used in hybrid light and laser modes to take advantage of laser accuracy and surface suitability alongside light texture capture [N2-F2]. This suggests that laser scanning can be adapted to some surface conditions, but it is not a universal fix for all waterlogged-wood problems.

Point-cloud processing is a key part of archaeological analysis. The evidence indicates that laser scanning produces a point cloud that can be processed into a 3D model or used in monitoring workflows [N2-R4]. It also notes that 3D scanning pipelines are provided to inform archaeological teams on a 3D digital and printing strategy [N2-F2]. More specifically, the evidence supports that point clouds can be aligned, registered, and combined into a single digital model, which is especially useful for monitoring and comparison over time [N2-F2]. The conservation-oriented evidence also shows that point clouds can be used to measure volume changes and assess dimensional stability after conservation [N3-R1]. This makes laser scanning well suited to quantitative analysis and repeatable monitoring.

Overall, laser scanning is strong for capturing precise 3D geometry and repeatable measurements on waterlogged wood, and it is especially useful when immersion or conservation liquids are present [N2-R3]. Its limitations include water-related optical interferences, surface condition variability, and the need for careful scanning environment control [N1-F1]. Point-cloud processing is essential for archaeological analysis, enabling 3D modeling, alignment, and quantitative comparison, which supports both documentation and conservation assessment [N2-F2][N3-R1].

The practical applications and case evidence for waterlogged wood show that both photogrammetry and laser scanning have been used to produce usable data, support interpretation and conservation, and enable repeated monitoring or time-lapse analysis. The evidence includes several examples that demonstrate these capabilities.

For photogrammetry, the evidence reports that photogrammetry has been used to monitor waterlogged wood in conservation liquids, with a stereo camera system attached to an automated biaxial measurement unit to acquire imagery [N1-F1]. The study specifically mentions the wooden track from the first century, subject to conservation, and states that the system was based on timing belts moving on the rim of a conservation tank of 6 x 1.5 m [N1-F1]. This is an explicit example of photogrammetry producing usable data in a conservation context. The evidence also notes that the system observed logs from a wooden track and used refraction correction and indirect flat lighting to mitigate turbidity [N1-F1]. This shows that photogrammetry supported interpretation and monitoring by capturing shape changes over time, while also addressing the environmental constraints of waterlogged wood [N1-F1].

For laser scanning, the evidence reports that terrestrial laser scanning enables accurate three-dimensional recording of fragile wet-preserved archaeological wood and that repeat scanning reveals immersion-related changes [N2-R3]. The same source states that the method is useful for recording worked archaeological wood and that repeat scanning can capture deformation or other changes over time [N2-R3]. Another source notes that structured-light 3D scanning and micro-computed tomography were used to analyse the dimensional stability of wood after conservation, including volume changes [N3-R1]. This indicates that laser scanning has been used not only for documentation but also for assessing conservation outcomes through volumetric analysis [N3-R1]. The evidence also mentions that repeat scanning reveals immersion-related changes, which is direct evidence of time-lapse or repeated monitoring [N2-R3].

The case-study evidence also shows how these methods supported interpretation, conservation, or publication. The case-study paper on waterlogged wood conservation used comparative analysis of conservation methods and included case studies such as the Paleolithic wooden point and a Roman barge, along with 3D scanning techniques such as CT and photogrammetry [N3-F3]. This demonstrates that 3D methods can support interpretation by enabling documentation and comparative analysis of different conservation strategies. The evidence also states that the digital data embedded in 3D surface and object models provides a wealth of supplementary information that cannot be captured, preserved, or documented through conventional techniques [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that these methods can enhance publication by providing detailed, non-invasive documentation [N3-F3].

There is also clear evidence of repeated monitoring or time-lapse analysis. The photogrammetry study explicitly discusses a monitoring approach using optical technologies, with an automated biaxial measurement unit and timing belts to acquire repeatable imagery over time [N1-F1]. The laser-scanning evidence similarly reports that repeat scanning reveals immersion-related changes [N2-R3]. The deformation-monitoring paper on the archaeological wooden shipwreck stern also provides a practical example of deformation monitoring using stereo DIC, which is closely related to the broader monitoring theme [N7-R1]. Although that example is not strictly photogrammetry, it shows that the field has developed workflows for tracking changes over time, which is consistent with the evidence provided for the aggregate [N7-R1].

Taken together, the case evidence shows that photogrammetry and laser scanning have both been used to produce usable data on waterlogged wood, support interpretation and conservation, and enable repeated monitoring or time-lapse analysis [N1-F1][N2-R3][N3-R1][N3-F3]. The evidence is especially strong for monitoring-oriented use cases, where the goal is to track shape, volume, or immersion-related changes over time [N1-F1][N2-R3].

When comparing photogrammetry and laser scanning for archaeological documentation, the evidence suggests that each method has distinct advantages and limitations, and that their suitability depends on the specific task, environment, and desired output. The comparison evidence indicates that photogrammetry can provide both 3D geometry and texture simultaneously, with accuracy values for each determined 3D point, although the exact details of that accuracy depend on the scene and setup [N5-R2]. It also states that photogrammetry compares to 3D scanning primarily in its dense-matching method and that photogrammetry offers more capabilities overall [N5-R3]. This implies that photogrammetry is preferable when texture preservation and detailed surface appearance are important, while laser scanning is preferable when high-precision geometry and repeatable point-cloud measurements are the priority [N5-R2][N5-R3].

Photogrammetry is generally preferable when the goal is to capture texture, color, and fine surface detail alongside geometry, especially when the object is accessible and the lighting and surface conditions can be controlled [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence also suggests that photogrammetry can be useful for documentation and visualization, because it produces textured 3D models that are rich in appearance information [N5-R2]. However, it is less preferable when the object is highly reflective, pale, or has poor surface texture, because those conditions can reduce the reliability of dense-matching [N2-F2]. In such cases, photogrammetry may require extensive calibration, lighting control, and careful image capture, which can increase effort and time [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Laser scanning is generally preferable when the goal is high-precision geometry, repeatable measurements, or point-cloud-based analysis [N2-F2][N2-R4]. The evidence notes that laser scanners are accurate, rapid, portable, and relatively low cost, and that they can be used in hybrid light and laser modes to combine laser accuracy with light texture capture [N2-F2]. It also states that terrestrial laser scanning can record fragile wet-preserved archaeological wood with repeat scanning revealing immersion-related changes [N2-R3]. This makes laser scanning a good choice for monitoring, volumetric analysis, and quantitative comparison over time [N2-R3][N3-R1]. However, laser scanning is less preferable when surface texture is the main documentation goal, because the evidence suggests that highly reflective or pale objects may fail to be captured even with altered strategies [N2-F2]. In conservation contexts, laser scanning is also vulnerable to water-related optical interferences, such as reflections and refraction, which can affect point-cloud quality [N1-F1].

Combining the methods can improve visualization and monitoring. The evidence indicates that photogrammetry can produce textured models, while laser scanning can produce precise point clouds [N5-R2][N2-R4]. Together, they can provide both detailed geometry and rich surface information, which is especially valuable for interpretation and conservation assessment [N5-R2][N2-R4]. The comparison evidence also suggests that photogrammetry’s dense-matching capability gives it broader overall capabilities than 3D scanning alone [N5-R3], while laser scanning offers better repeatability and precision for quantitative analysis [N2-F2]. This combination can therefore support richer visualization and more robust monitoring, especially when the goal is to combine appearance with metric accuracy [N5-R2][N2-F2].

The trade-offs in cost, time, and data quality are important. The evidence notes that laser scanning is relatively low cost, rapid, portable, and user-friendly [N2-F2]. Photogrammetry can also be rapid and portable, but it often requires careful setup, lighting control, and post-processing to achieve high accuracy [N1-F1][N2-F2]. In terms of data quality, laser scanning is often favored for precise geometry and repeatable measurements, while photogrammetry is often favored for texture and appearance [N5-R2][N5-R3]. However, photogrammetry may require more time and effort in difficult conditions, and its results can be degraded by poor lighting, poor texture, or refraction [N1-F1]. Overall, the best choice depends on whether the priority is texture/visualization, precision/monitoring, or a combination of both [N5-R2][N5-R3][N2-F2].

Monitoring gains from 3D methods for waterlogged wood come from their ability to track shape, volume, and deformation over time in a non-invasive and repeatable way. The evidence shows that 3D methods can be used to monitor changes in waterlogged wood through repeated scanning or imaging, which is especially important because waterlogged wood is prone to deformation and decay if not stabilized immediately after recovery [N1-F1]. The laser-scanning evidence also indicates that terrestrial laser scanning enables accurate three-dimensional recording of fragile wet-preserved archaeological wood and that repeat scanning reveals immersion-related changes [N2-R3]. This directly supports the idea that 3D methods can capture temporal variation in the object’s condition [N2-R3].

For shape and volume tracking, the evidence highlights that laser scanning can measure volume changes after conservation and that structured-light 3D scanning was used to analyse dimensional stability [N3-R1]. The same source notes that repeat scanning reveals immersion-related changes, which implies that volume and overall shape can be monitored over time [N2-R3]. The evidence also mentions that point-cloud processing can be used to align and compare scans, which is essential for quantitative shape and volume tracking [N2-F2]. This means that 3D methods are not just static documentation tools but also dynamic monitoring systems that can track how an object changes physically [N2-F2][N3-R1].

For deformation tracking, the evidence includes stereo DIC as a deformation-monitoring method, which tracks movement of the surface pattern during an experiment [N7-R5]. The case-study evidence for the archaeological wooden shipwreck stern shows a practical and effective deformation monitoring system based on stereo DIC for 3D deformation evaluation [N7-R1]. Although this example is not laser scanning, it is consistent with the broader monitoring theme and shows that 3D deformation methods can be adapted to waterlogged wood contexts [N7-R1]. The photogrammetry evidence also notes that the system used special target heads and refraction correction to capture deformation points [N1-F1], which indicates that photogrammetry can be used for deformation monitoring when combined with controlled hardware and image-processing workflows [N1-F1].

In terms of monitoring tasks best suited to photogrammetry or laser scanning, the evidence suggests a division of labor. Laser scanning is especially well suited to quantitative monitoring tasks where high-precision geometry, repeatable measurements, and point-cloud-based analysis are needed [N2-F2][N2-R3]. It is useful for tracking volume changes, immersion-related changes, and dimensional stability [N2-R3][N3-R1]. Photogrammetry, by contrast, is better suited to tasks where texture, color, and surface appearance are important, such as documenting the visible condition and capturing the overall shape in a more visually informative way [N1-F1][N5-R2]. ## How advances in photogrammetry and laser scanning have enhanced visualization and monitoring of waterlogged archaeological wood

Waterlogged archaeological wood is a highly challenging material to study and conserve because it is prone to deformation and decay if not stabilized immediately after recovery [N1-F1]. Advances in photogrammetry and laser scanning have therefore been especially valuable, not only because they can capture the object’s form and surface detail, but because they can do so in a way that supports repeated monitoring and conservation decision-making over time [N1-F1][N2-R3]. The two methods are complementary rather than interchangeable: photogrammetry excels at texture and visualization, while laser scanning excels at precise geometry and repeatable measurement [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-R2]. Together, they have greatly enhanced both the *visualization* and *monitoring* of waterlogged wood.

### 1) Photogrammetry enhances visualization by capturing shape, texture, and color

Photogrammetry can reliably capture the overall geometry and texture of waterlogged archaeological wood, including fine surface details and color information, provided the imaging system is calibrated appropriately [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that photogrammetry can provide “high resolution and accuracy” if calibrated, and that it is useful for monitoring waterlogged wood in conservation liquids [N1-F1]. This makes it especially valuable for visualization, because it can produce textured 3D models that are rich in appearance information [N5-R2]. In practice, photogrammetry has been used to monitor waterlogged wood in conservation liquids, with a stereo camera system attached to an automated biaxial measurement unit to acquire imagery [N1-F1]. The system used special target heads and refraction correction to capture deformation points, showing that photogrammetry can be adapted to waterlogged-wood constraints [N1-F1].

A major limitation is that waterlogged wood often lacks rich texture, which complicates Structure-from-Motion (SfM) techniques [N1-F1]. The source also notes that water and conservation liquids introduce optical interferences such as reflections, chromatic aberration, refraction at air–water interfaces, and turbidity, all of which degrade image quality [N1-F1]. These issues are especially severe in a multimedia environment where refraction and scale definition are critical [N1-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that ambient lighting can be excluded or controlled in specialized setups, such as nighttime measurements, to reduce interference [N1-F1]. This shows that visualization quality depends heavily on lighting, refraction correction, scale bars, and relative orientation constraints [N1-F1].

Photogrammetry is therefore best when the goal is to capture texture, color, and surface appearance alongside geometry [N5-R2]. Its visualization advantage is that it can produce detailed, visually informative models, which is especially useful for interpretation and publication [N3-F3]. However, it is less reliable when the object is highly reflective, pale, or has poor surface texture, because those conditions can reduce the reliability of dense-matching [N2-F2].

### 2) Laser scanning enhances monitoring by capturing precise geometry and repeatable measurements

Laser scanning is especially strong for capturing precise 3D geometry and repeatable measurements on waterlogged wood [N2-F2]. The evidence shows that terrestrial laser scanning enables accurate three-dimensional recording of fragile wet-preserved archaeological wood, and that repeat scanning reveals immersion-related changes [N2-R3]. Another source notes that laser scanners use laser lines to measure distance to points on the object and that modern scanners are accurate, rapid, portable, and relatively low cost [N2-F2]. This makes laser scanning especially suitable for monitoring fragile objects that may not tolerate physical contact [N2-R4].

Laser scanning can reliably capture surface detail and can be used to track changes over time, which is central to monitoring waterlogged wood [N2-R3]. The evidence also indicates that point clouds can be processed into a 3D model or used in monitoring workflows [N2-R4]. More specifically, it notes that 3D scanning pipelines are provided to inform archaeological teams on a 3D digital and printing strategy [N2-F2]. This pipeline-oriented approach is important because it allows repeated scans to be aligned, registered, and compared over time [N2-F2].

A major limitation is that waterlogged wood is often submerged or surrounded by conservation liquids, which can affect the scanning environment and introduce challenges such as reflections, refraction, and turbidity [N1-F1]. The evidence also emphasizes that waterlogged wood is prone to deformation and decay if not stabilized immediately after recovery [N1-F1], meaning scanning must often be done in controlled conservation settings rather than in open-air conditions. Additionally, the conservation liquid surrounding the wood can over the course of treatment cause deformation, rotation, local degradation, and other optical interferences on images observing the wood [N1-F1]. This means that laser scanning is sensitive to the physical condition of the wood and the surrounding liquid [N1-F1].

Surface condition and scan environment also matter. The evidence notes that highly reflective objects or pale objects with black areas may fail to be captured even with altered strategies [N2-F2]. For waterlogged wood, the surface may be damp, wet, or covered by conservation fluids, which can affect reflectivity and scanning consistency [N1-F1]. The source also states that laser scanners can be used in hybrid light and laser modes to take advantage of laser accuracy and surface suitability alongside light texture capture [N2-F2]. This shows that laser scanning can be adapted to some surface conditions, but it is not a universal fix for all waterlogged-wood problems [N2-F2].

### 3) Practical applications and case evidence show both methods are used in real conservation contexts

The practical applications and case evidence show that both photogrammetry and laser scanning have been used to produce usable data, support interpretation and conservation, and enable repeated monitoring or time-lapse analysis [N1-F1][N2-R3][N3-R1][N3-F3]. The evidence includes examples such as photogrammetry monitoring waterlogged wood in conservation liquids with an automated biaxial measurement unit and timing belts on a conservation tank [N1-F1]. For laser scanning, the evidence reports that terrestrial laser scanning enables accurate three-dimensional recording of fragile wet-preserved archaeological wood and that repeat scanning reveals immersion-related changes [N2-R3]. It also notes that structured-light 3D scanning and micro-computed tomography were used to analyse the dimensional stability of wood after conservation, including volume changes [N3-R1]. This demonstrates that these methods are not just static documentation tools but are also used to assess conservation outcomes over time [N3-R1].

The case-study evidence also shows how these methods support interpretation, conservation, or publication. The case-study paper on waterlogged wood conservation used comparative analysis of conservation methods and included case studies such as the Paleolithic wooden point and a Roman barge, along with 3D scanning techniques such as CT and photogrammetry [N3-F3]. The evidence also states that the digital data embedded in 3D surface and object models provides a wealth of supplementary information that cannot be captured, preserved, or documented through conventional techniques [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that these methods can enhance publication by providing detailed, non-invasive documentation [N3-F3].

Evidence of repeated monitoring or time-lapse analysis is explicit. The photogrammetry study reports a monitoring approach using optical technologies with an automated biaxial measurement unit and timing belts to acquire repeatable imagery over time [N1-F1]. The laser-scanning evidence similarly reports that repeat scanning reveals immersion-related changes [N2-R3]. Although that example is not strictly photogrammetry, it shows that the field has developed workflows for tracking changes over time, which is consistent with the evidence provided for the aggregate [N7-R1].

### 4) Monitoring-specific gains: tracking shape, volume, deformation, and supporting conservation decisions

The monitoring-specific gains from 3D methods for waterlogged wood are substantial. They allow the object to be tracked in shape, volume, and deformation over time in a non-invasive and repeatable way [N1-F1][N2-R3]. The evidence shows that 3D methods can be used to monitor changes in waterlogged wood through repeated scanning or imaging, which is especially important because waterlogged wood is prone to deformation and decay if not stabilized immediately after recovery [N1-F1]. This directly supports the idea that 3D methods can capture temporal variation in the object’s condition [N2-R3].

For shape and volume tracking, the evidence highlights that laser scanning can measure volume changes after conservation and that structured-light 3D scanning was used to analyse dimensional stability [N3-R1]. The same source notes that repeat scanning reveals immersion-related changes, which implies that volume and overall shape can be monitored over time [N2-R3]. The evidence also mentions that point-cloud processing can be used to align and compare scans, which is essential for quantitative shape and volume tracking [N2-F2]. This means that 3D methods are not just static documentation tools but also dynamic monitoring systems that can track how an object changes physically [N2-F2][N3-R1].

For deformation tracking, the evidence includes stereo DIC as a deformation-monitoring method, which tracks movement of the surface pattern during an experiment [N7-R5]. The case-study evidence for the archaeological wooden shipwreck stern shows a practical and effective deformation monitoring system based on stereo DIC for 3D deformation evaluation [N7-R1]. Although this example is not laser scanning, it is consistent with the broader monitoring theme and shows that 3D deformation methods can be adapted to waterlogged wood contexts [N7-R1]. The photogrammetry evidence also notes that the system used special target heads and refraction correction to capture deformation points [N1-F1], which indicates that photogrammetry can be used for deformation monitoring when combined with controlled hardware and image-processing workflows [N1-F1].

Monitoring tasks are best suited to the strengths of each method. Laser scanning is especially well suited to quantitative monitoring tasks where high-precision geometry, repeatable measurements, and point-cloud-based analysis are needed [N2-F2][N2-R3]. It is useful for tracking volume changes, immersion-related changes, and dimensional stability [N2-R3][N3-R1]. In conservation, such data can guide decisions about whether to continue a treatment, adjust conditions, or intervene more aggressively [N1-F1][N3-R1].

### 5) Comparison and integration: when each method is preferable and how they combine

The comparison evidence shows that photogrammetry and laser scanning are not one-size-fits-all: each has distinct advantages and limitations, and their suitability depends on the specific task, environment, and desired output [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Photogrammetry is preferable when the goal is to capture texture, color, and fine surface detail alongside geometry, especially when the object is accessible and the lighting and surface conditions can be controlled [N5-R2][N5-R3]. It is less preferable when the object is highly reflective, pale, or has poor surface texture, because those conditions can reduce the reliability of dense-matching [N2-F2]. In such cases, photogrammetry may require extensive calibration, lighting control, and careful image capture, which can increase effort and time [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Laser scanning is preferable when the goal is high-precision geometry, repeatable measurements, or point-cloud-based analysis [N2-F2][N2-R4]. It is especially suitable for monitoring, volumetric analysis, and quantitative comparison over time [N2-R3][N3-R1]. However, it is less preferable when surface texture is the main documentation goal, because the evidence suggests that highly reflective or pale objects may fail to be captured even with altered strategies [N2-F2]. In conservation contexts, laser scanning is also vulnerable to water-related optical interferences, such as reflections and refraction, which can affect point-cloud quality [N1-F1].

The comparison evidence also suggests that photogrammetry’s dense-matching capability gives it broader overall capabilities than 3D scanning alone [N5-R3], while laser scanning offers better repeatability and precision for quantitative analysis [N2-F2]. Taken together, advances in photogrammetry and laser scanning have transformed the visualization and monitoring of waterlogged archaeological wood in three ways:

1. **They allow detailed documentation of shape and texture**, even under challenging waterlogged conditions [N1-F1][N2-F2].  
2. **They enable repeated monitoring over time**, supporting the tracking of deformation, volume change, and immersion-related changes [N1-F1][N2-R3][N3-R1].  
3. **They support conservation decision-making** by providing objective, repeatable evidence of how the object is changing [N3-R1][N1-F1].

For conservation practice, these advances mean that waterlogged wood can be studied without exposing it to unnecessary risk, and that treatments can be assessed more precisely over time [N1-F1][N3-R1]. For publication and interpretation, they mean that the object can be presented in rich, textured 3D form, preserving details that would otherwise be lost or hard to capture [N3-F3]. In short, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: advances in photogrammetry and laser scanning have greatly enhanced the visualization and monitoring of waterlogged archaeological wood by making it possible to document, track, and conserve these fragile materials in a more precise, repeatable, and non-invasive way [N1-F1][N2-R3][N3-R1][N5-R2].
